t: Subsequences with a Unique Middle Mode II
o: Count 5-element subsequences whose middle element (3rd smallest index) is the UNIQUE mode. Enumerate the middle index j with value v; we pick 2 elements from the left and 2 from the right. If v appears a total of 1 time it can't be a strict mode; totals 2, 3, 4, 5 each impose conditions: total 2 requires the three other elements pairwise distinct; totals 3–5 are automatically unique. Sweeping j left to right with running per-value counts on each side and aggregate statistics (Σ C(c,2), Σ cL·cR, Σ cL·C2(cR), …) makes every case O(1) amortized, for O(n) total.
k: Fix the middle index j (value v); with cl, cr = v-counts on each side, the cases are: 1 extra v (needs 3 distinct non-v), 2 extras (any 2 non-v), 3 extras (any 1 non-v), 4 extras (none).
Distinctness counting reduces to global aggregates: Σ C(cnt,2) per side, Σ cntL·cntR, and Σ cntL·C2(cntR) (and its mirror), all maintainable in O(1) per element move.
Each element moves from the right pool to the left pool exactly once, giving an O(n) sweep with hash maps.

a.i: Enumerate all index 5-combinations, tally counts, and check that the middle value is the strict maximum-frequency element. Establishes semantics; far too slow for n = 10^5.
s: Count values; require count(middle value) strictly greater than every other count

a.n: Approach 2: O(n) sweep with count aggregates
a.i: For middle j with value v, let cl/cr be v's counts left/right and Ln/Rn the non-v counts. Contributions: (a) one extra v from either side times the number of ways to pick the remaining non-v elements with all-distinct values — expressed via D2(Q)=C2(|Q|)−Σ C2(cQ) and cross-aggregates X=Σ cL·cR, Y1=Σ cL·C2(cR), Y2=Σ cR·C2(cL); (b) two extras: C2(cl)·C2(Rn) + C2(cr)·C2(Ln) + cl·cr·Ln·Rn; (c) three extras: C2(cl)·cr·Rn + cl·C2(cr)·Ln; (d) four extras: C2(cl)·C2(cr). An `apply(x, dl, dr)` helper updates all aggregates when an element switches pools.
s: Load all counts into the right pool; sweep j left to right
Before processing j, apply(v, 0, -1) to move nums[j] out of the right pool
Add the four-case contribution for (v, cl, cr, Ln, Rn) using the aggregates; then apply(v, +1, 0)

c.python:
class Solution:
    def subsequencesWithMiddleMode(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        from collections import defaultdict
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        n = len(nums)
        cntL = defaultdict(int); cntR = defaultdict(int)
        for x in nums: cntR[x] += 1
        agg = {'spl': 0, 'spr': 0, 'X': 0, 'Y1': 0, 'Y2': 0}
        def C2(x): return x * (x - 1) // 2 if x > 1 else 0
        def upd(x, dl, dr):
            a, b = cntL[x], cntR[x]
            agg['spl'] -= C2(a); agg['spr'] -= C2(b)
            agg['X'] -= a * b; agg['Y1'] -= C2(a) * b; agg['Y2'] -= C2(b) * a
            cntL[x] += dl; cntR[x] += dr
            a, b = cntL[x], cntR[x]
            agg['spl'] += C2(a); agg['spr'] += C2(b)
            agg['X'] += a * b; agg['Y1'] += C2(a) * b; agg['Y2'] += C2(b) * a
        ans = 0
        for j in range(n):
            v = nums[j]
            upd(v, 0, -1)
            cl, cr = cntL[v], cntR[v]
            Ln, Rn = j - cl, (n - 1 - j) - cr
            fL = (C2(Rn) - agg['spr']) * Ln - agg['X'] * Rn + agg['Y1']
            fR = (C2(Ln) - agg['spl']) * Rn - agg['X'] * Ln + agg['Y2']
            res = (cl * fL + cr * fR + cl * cr * Ln * Rn
                   + C2(cl) * C2(Rn) + C2(cr) * C2(Ln)
                   + C2(cl) * cr * Rn + cl * C2(cr) * Ln
                   + C2(cl) * C2(cr))
            ans = (ans + res) % MOD
            upd(v, 1, 0)
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — one hash-map update pair per element, all case arithmetic O(1)
a.sp: O(n) for the count hash maps

w: Validate against the samples: all-equal arrays give Σ_j C2(j)·C2(n−1−j) (6 for n = 6), all-distinct gives 0, and [1,2,2,3,3,4] gives 4. The delicate parts: (1) the middle is positional (index 2 of the subsequence), not the median value; (2) total v-count of 1 can never win, and total 2 forces the other three values to be pairwise distinct; (3) keep all intermediate products in 64-bit before reducing mod 1e9+7. Follow-up: generalize to subsequences of size 2k+1 with a unique middle mode — the same case analysis extends with more aggregate statistics.
